title: The Goodman Trio as the first public interracial group
summary: Wilson says the 1936 Goodman Trio at the Congress Hotel put racial mixing on stage on equal terms, where earlier acts used a shadow-boy routine.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well, a lot of the exposure, I think, came from the Goodman, the spotlight thing was on the Goodman Trio because we were the first interracial organization in this country - we were 10 years before the sporting world, when the Goodman Trio came out of a recording studio, for years where there had been many mixed bands in the recording studio for years, but nobody played it live.
until the Goodman Trio was formed at the Congress Hotel in Chicago in 1936, when we played -- and the public spotlight was really on me, and Krupa and them.

Yeah. We had a tremendous, big audience watching this new thing of racial mixing on an equal basis. Because before that, the racial mixing would be like Ted Lewis doing "Me and My Shadow" -- he would prance around the stage signing "Me and My Shadow" and the little negro boy would be following him and imitating every motion and be the shadow.
That category of appearing was widely known. But in a lot of states and cities, it was illegal for the two races to be on the stage at the same time.
There were a lot of states like that.
